standard_text: Genetic variation and natural selection; gene pools and allele frequencies; the Hardy–Weinberg principle; genetic drift, founder effect, bottlenecks and gene flow; speciation and reproductive isolation; evidence for evolution. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 3: Heredity and continuity of life)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Biology worksheets on evolution: natural selection, allele frequencies, Hardy–Weinberg, genetic drift, the founder effect, gene flow, speciation and evidence for evolution. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a gene pool.
body_html:
How to think about it

Natural selection acts on heritable variation: individuals with favourable alleles survive and reproduce more, so those alleles increase. Genetic drift (chance, strongest in small populations), the founder effect, bottlenecks and gene flow also change allele frequencies.

When populations are isolated (for example by Bass Strait) and diverge until they can no longer interbreed, new species form. Evidence for evolution includes fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biogeography and DNA comparisons.

Example

q² = 0.09. Find q and the carrier frequency.

q = 0.3, p = 0.7

2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3

Answer: 0.42

Example

A ring of 10 survivors founds a new population. Which effect?

a few individuals start a population

Answer: the founder effect

Common mistakes

  • Saying individuals evolve: populations do.
  • Thinking organisms change because they need to.
  • Using q² as the carrier frequency.

faq.q: What are the conditions for Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?
faq.a: A large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration and no selection. Real populations rarely meet them, so frequencies change.

faq.q: Why is Australian wildlife so useful for studying evolution?
faq.a: Long isolation produced adaptive radiation of marsupials and convergent evolution with placental mammals elsewhere.

c: unrelated species evolve similar features because they live in similar environments

items.q: What is allopatric speciation?

items.e: Mutation, selection and drift act separately.

items.q: What is disruptive selection?
c: both extreme phenotypes are favoured over the middle

items.q: What is sympatric speciation?
c: new species form in the same area, for example through reproductive isolation
items.e: It can be caused by polyploidy or behaviour changes.

items.q: What is reproductive isolation?
c: changes that stop two populations interbreeding to give fertile offspring
items.e: It can be seasonal, mechanical or behavioural.
